vignette:
She is eighty now, a compact woman with careful hands and the calm, practical manner of someone who has spent a lifetime ushering other people through fear. For more than fifty years she works as a midwife, first in a crowded district hospital in Africa and later in a smaller clinic near the neighborhood where she and her husband raise their children. Even in retirement, women still come to her gate for advice. She laughs easily when she talks about babies, about stubborn first labors and relieved grandmothers, but the laughter disappears when the conversation turns to roads.

The accident happens twelve years ago, on a hot afternoon at the end of the rainy season. She is traveling back from a rural health post with a younger nurse after a long delivery that has kept them overnight. She remembers the red mud at the roadside, the smell of wet earth, the heavy sky. They are tired and eager to get home. A truck coming from the opposite direction skids as it tries to pass another vehicle. She sees it veer across the road toward them. There is only a second to understand that it is too large and too close. She hears the nurse beside her say, “Mama,” and then there is metal folding, glass exploding inward, her body thrown hard against the door.

What she remembers next comes in bright, disconnected flashes: blood on her uniform, the steering wheel bent at an unnatural angle, the taste of diesel and dirt in her mouth. She cannot move her leg at first and believes she will die there before anyone reaches them. She hears people shouting outside, but the voices seem far away. Her chest feels crushed. She tries to pray and cannot find the words. What terrifies her most is not pain but the certainty, in those moments, that her life is ending in a ditch by the road, with strangers pulling at twisted metal while she is still awake inside it.

She survives with broken ribs, a fractured ankle, and deep bruising. The younger nurse survives too, though she is badly injured. In the hospital, everyone tells her she is blessed. Her husband sits by her bed and feeds her soup. Her children come in shifts. Colleagues from the maternity ward visit with fruit and stories. She thanks God with them and tries to speak as if the worst is over. But at night, when the ward quiets, she hears again the scream of brakes and the bursting glass. She jerks awake certain the truck is entering the room. Her heart races so violently she presses her hand to her chest and waits for it to slow. If someone drops a metal tray in the corridor, her whole body leaps before she can stop it.

When she is physically stronger, she expects herself to return to the woman she has always been—capable, busy, unafraid of emergencies. Instead she begins avoiding the road where the crash happened, then avoiding cars altogether. At first she tells people her ankle still pains her, which is partly true. Her husband drives her to the clinic, but she grips the seat and watches every approaching vehicle, sucking in breath whenever a truck appears. Sometimes she shouts without meaning to, warning him to slow down, to stop, to move aside. If rain begins, she begs to turn back. Eventually she starts refusing outreach visits to distant villages, though she had once been known for going anywhere a woman was in labor. She feels ashamed each time she sends a younger midwife in her place.

The memories do not stay politely in the past. They push in while she is boiling water, folding laundry, checking a newborn’s latch. A flash of sunlight on a windshield can bring back the impact so sharply that for a moment she smells diesel again. She becomes watchful in a way that exhausts her. In church she chooses an aisle seat so she can leave easily. In markets she scans for exits. At home she startles when her grandchildren run up behind her. She hates this most of all, the way her body reacts before her mind can reassure it. She used to be the steady one in every family crisis. Now she feels her nerves are “sitting on top of the skin.”

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. She dreads bedtime because dreams place her back inside the vehicle, trapped and unable to breathe. Some nights she wakes shouting for help, and her husband turns on the light and reminds her where she is. In the morning she is embarrassed and quiet. She has begun to keep many things to herself because she is tired of hearing that she should be grateful simply to be alive. She is grateful. That is what makes her guilt so confusing. Women in her care survive hemorrhage, obstructed labor, stillbirth, poverty. She has always told them that survival is strength. Yet after the accident, she finds herself weeping alone in the bathroom, angry at her own fear, angry that one moment on one road has made the world feel permanently unsafe.

Now, even years later, she measures distance less by kilometers than by whether she can bear the journey. She still sits with pregnant women in her front room, still places an experienced palm on a tense belly and speaks with authority. But if a truck backfires outside, her voice falters midsentence. She pauses, listens, and waits for her body to learn again what her mind already knows: that she is here, in the present, and not on that road.
